archetype.name: Dual-Threat (power-runner, vertical passer)
archetype.definition: A big-bodied passer who wins with a downfield arm and doubles as his offense's short-yardage and red-zone runner, so his production comes from two separate engines.

report.headline: Allen's most vertical passing year, with his legs doing the scoring near the goal line
report.take:
Seven games in, Josh Allen is the same two-engine quarterback he has been for years, with the passing engine tuned more vertically. His 8.75 yards per attempt ranks 4th of 47 and sits well above last year's 7.97, even though his completion rate dropped from 69.3% to 65.9%. That trade is deliberate. His aggressiveness (throws into tight windows) is up 2.4 points on last year, and the throws of 10+ air yards are carrying the passing game: 0.548 EPA per attempt with 8 of his 11 touchdowns. On the 32 deep attempts he completes only 40.6%, but those throws produce 0.792 EPA each and a +8.5 CPOE. He isn't just chucking it up. He is hitting throws the model doesn't expect him to hit.

The fantasy line, 26.8 PPR a game and 1st at the position, rests as much on his legs as his arm. He leads all qualifiers in rushing yards. His 19 scrambles average 1.17 EPA and 13 of them moved the chains. He also has nine rushing touchdowns, seven on designed runs that average just 2.64 yards a carry but succeed 67.9% of the time. Those are sneaks and goal-line keepers, not open-field runs. That is also why his red-zone passing looks so poor: 47.2% completions, -7.4 CPOE and essentially zero EPA. Buffalo doesn't need him to throw there because the quarterback run is the red-zone play.

The numbers also show the price of the style. His 2.4% interception rate ranks 33rd of 47, he has four turnover-worthy fumbles on top of the five picks, and his bad-throw rate swings wildly by game (26.9% against the Chargers, 27.8% in Los Angeles, 6.7% twice). None of that is new. He finished in the bottom tier for interceptions in 2021, 2022 and 2023, and it is the cost of a quarterback who keeps attacking. Sacks are the same story. He has been pressured on only 17.5% of dropbacks (7th of 38), but when pressure arrives he holds and gets dropped 31.6% of the time, rank 26. That is better than last year's 40.4% and well short of the 14-19% he posted from 2021 to 2024.

The context helps him. Buffalo has the league's top offense by EPA, but its defense ranks 28th, so most of his games have been shootouts that keep him throwing in close scores, where his 0.222 EPA per play holds steady. The offense actually passes less than the situation predicts (-3.5, 24th), so his volume isn't inflated. The efficiency is real, and the rushing touchdowns are the part most likely to cool.

strengths.title: Downfield accuracy driving efficiency
strengths.body: His throws of 20+ air yards produce 0.792 EPA per attempt with a +8.5 CPOE. He is completing difficult deep balls at a rate well above expectation, not just collecting a few lucky bombs. His higher aggressiveness explains both the higher yards per attempt and the lower completion rate. The exact deep EPA will drift down on 32 attempts, but the trait matches his career. He has finished top-10 in EPA per play in six of the last seven seasons.

strengths.title: Scrambles and keepers as a second offense
strengths.body: He leads qualifiers in rushing yards. His scrambles average 1.17 EPA, so when a play breaks down he turns it into a gain rather than a loss. The designed runs are short-yardage tools that succeed about two-thirds of the time and have produced seven touchdowns. The rushing role is sustainable because it has held for eight seasons; the touchdown count is not.

strengths.title: Steady in close games and late
strengths.body: Most of his snaps have come within one score, and he is still adding 0.222 EPA per play there. In close fourth quarters his EPA rises to 0.396. His production isn't built in garbage time, which matters because Buffalo's defense keeps games tight.

concerns.title: Turnovers are part of the package
concerns.body: His interception rate ranks 33rd of 47 and spiked to 3.4% over his last five games. He also has four turnover-worthy fumbles. This is a long-running trait: he ranked near the bottom for interceptions in 2021 through 2023. It is partly the cost of his aggressive downfield throwing. Expect it to keep producing the occasional two-pick game, as against the Chargers.

concerns.title: Holding the ball under pressure
concerns.body: He is rarely pressured, but 31.6% of his pressures end in sacks. That is better than last year's 40.4%, but far from the low-to-high teens he ran from 2021 to 2024. Some of it is the price of extending plays to create scrambles, which mostly pay off. It becomes a real problem against a defense that gets home, especially with a starting tackle out.

concerns.title: Red-zone passing is flat
concerns.body: Inside the 20 he completes 47.2% of his passes with a -7.4 CPOE and adds nothing by EPA. The scoring has come on keepers instead. This matters less than it looks while the quarterback run keeps working. But if the rushing touchdowns slow down, his passing has to finish drives it hasn't been finishing.

trend.note: A dip in Weeks 3-4 (negative passing EPA, two interceptions and four sacks against the Chargers) drags the five-game window down. The last three games, all wins, are right back at his season efficiency with more rushing yards per game. Out of the bye he threw for 289 yards against Baltimore.

nextGame.headline: League's best pass defense, with Allen's right tackle out
nextGame.body:
Minnesota is the hardest matchup on his schedule so far. It ranks 1st in defensive EPA, pass EPA, success rate, hit rate and sack rate, and allows the fewest fantasy points and touchdowns per game to quarterbacks. That defense attacks the one area where he is vulnerable, holding the ball under pressure. Offenses also run far more than usual against the Vikings, the strongest run funnel in the league, and its explosive-run rate allowed ranks 30th. Its deep-pass defense (10th) is also softer than its short-area coverage (6th). The paths for Allen are his legs and a few downfield shots, not a high-volume passing day. The 45.5 total is lower than every total in his game log.

Availability cuts both ways. Right tackle Spencer Brown, an 88%-snap starter, is out, and his backup faces the league's best pass rush. DJ Moore (knee) says he's okay, and Joshua Palmer (hamstring) is questionable, but Shakir, Kincaid and Coleman carry the passing game anyway. On Minnesota's side, quarterback Kyler Murray is being evaluated for a hamstring injury and left tackle Christian Darrisaw is questionable, on an offense that already ranks 29th. If Murray sits, Buffalo can likely lean on the run with a lead. That would limit Allen's passing volume but not his goal-line work. The game is indoors, so weather isn't a factor.

keyMatchups.title: Backup right tackle versus top pass rush
keyMatchups.body: Minnesota leads the league in hit rate and sack rate, and Buffalo loses its starting right tackle. Allen converts too many pressures into sacks. Expect more pressure than his usual low rate, and with it a higher sack count unless he speeds up his release.

keyMatchups.title: Run funnel suits his keepers
keyMatchups.body: Offenses pass far less than usual against this defense, and it gives up explosive runs at one of the highest rates. Buffalo's run game ranks 3rd by EPA. Allen's scrambles and designed runs are the likeliest way his fantasy floor holds up against an otherwise stingy defense.

keyMatchups.title: Kincaid runs into the best TE defense
keyMatchups.body: Dalton Kincaid has been one of his most efficient targets. But Minnesota allows the lowest EPA per play to tight ends in the league, while its defense against WR1s ranks only 24th. Expect Allen's productive throws to shift toward the receivers outside, Coleman's downfield routes especially.

nextGame.watch: Whether Allen gets the ball out on time against Minnesota's rush with a backup at right tackle, or holds it and takes the sacks that stall drives.

restOfSeason.body:
The passing efficiency looks largely real. He has finished top-10 in EPA per play almost every year, the higher aggressiveness explains the yards-per-attempt jump, and Buffalo's weak defense should keep him throwing in competitive games. The deep-ball figure on 32 attempts will likely cool, and the interceptions will keep coming at roughly the rate they always have. Expect something like 225-265 passing yards and 1.3-1.8 touchdown passes a game, with good and bad passing days alternating.

The rushing touchdowns are what will regress. Seven designed-run scores in seven games is a short-yardage role at an unsustainable hit rate, so the number should drop toward roughly one touchdown every other game. The rushing yardage and scramble value should hold. That still leaves him at or near the top of the position in fantasy, just closer to 22-26 points a game than 27.
swingFactors: Pass protection while Spencer Brown is out
Whether Buffalo's defense keeps forcing shootouts

confidence.note: Seven games and small deep-ball and red-zone samples, but eight seasons of consistent career baseline.
